title: Law & Your Rights · Episode 3
chapters: Making a complaint that actually gets results
Working on an ABN: contractor or employee
Making a will, and why it matters

units.t: Law & Your Rights. Episode three.
In this episode: Making a complaint that actually gets results, Your rights at work, Working on an ABN: contractor or employee and Making a will, and why it matters.
Part one. Making a complaint that actually gets results.
Knowing your rights is one thing; getting a business to honour them is another.
Here is the step by step path from polite email to independent ombudsman.
Goal and evidence.
Consider a washing machine that dies a fortnight after its warranty ends.
Angry calls get nowhere; clarity works.
Write down what went wrong, when, and what you want: a repair, replacement, refund or compensation.
Then check Australian Consumer Law.
Its consumer guarantees mean goods must be of acceptable quality and last a reasonable time, regardless of any manufacturer's warranty, and a major failure gives you a choice of remedy.
The ACCC, accc.
gov.
au, explains this in plain English.
Gather proof of purchase, photos or video of the fault, and any packaging.
Start a log of every call, email and visit, with the date, the person and what they said or promised, including any sales claims.
It makes your complaint precise, and shows you tried to resolve things first.
This is general information, not legal advice.
Complain in writing.
Most problems are fixed at the first step, so give the business a genuine chance.
Ask to speak with someone who can make decisions, often a manager or the complaints team rather than front counter staff.
Be polite, specific and firm.
If that does not work, put your complaint in writing by email or letter.
Briefly set out what you bought, the problem, what you have done so far and the remedy you want.
Refer to the consumer guarantees if relevant, and give a reasonable deadline, such as 14 days, for a response.
Many large businesses must have an internal dispute resolution process, and asking for your complaint to be formally logged often moves it to more senior people.
Fair trading and ombudsmen.
For most goods and services, contact your state fair trading agency, such as NSW Fair Trading or Consumer Affairs Victoria.
They can advise and may contact the business for you.
The ACCC enforces the law nationally but generally does not resolve individual disputes.

Several industries have free, independent ombudsman schemes: the Telecommunications Industry Ombudsman for phone and internet, the Australian Financial Complaints Authority for banks, insurers and super funds, and state energy and water ombudsmen.
Most require you to complain to the business first.
The scheme sends your complaint back to senior staff for a last chance to fix it, and many settle there.
If not, it investigates and may recommend or decide an outcome.
With AFCA, a decision you accept can bind the business, and you can still go to court if you reject it.
Tribunals and chargebacks.
If no ombudsman covers the business and the fair trading agency cannot resolve it, a state tribunal or local court can hear consumer claims.
Examples include NCAT in New South Wales, VCAT in Victoria and QCAT in Queensland.
Small claims processes are designed to be cheaper and less formal than ordinary courts, though there is usually a filing fee and you present your own case with your evidence.
Separately, if you paid by credit or debit card and the goods never arrived or the business has collapsed, ask your bank about a chargeback.
Card schemes have rules for disputed transactions, and banks set time limits for requests, so contact them as soon as you realise there is a problem.
Tone and persistence.
The most effective complainers are rarely the loudest.
Staff who are shouted at tend to follow the script; staff who are treated respectfully often look for a way to help.
Keep messages short and factual, repeat your requested remedy clearly, and do not accept vague promises without a date.
If you are offered less than you asked for, consider whether it is fair rather than rejecting it on principle, since time and stress have costs too.
Public reviews and social media posts can attract attention, but stick to accurate facts to avoid defamation risks.
Finally, report scams and misleading conduct to the ACCC or Scamwatch, even if you get your money back.
It helps protect the next customer.
The key idea: Decide the outcome you want, know your consumer guarantees, and keep evidence and a log.
Part two. Your rights at work.
Minimum pay, leave, a safe workplace and protection from unfair sacking aren't favours from your boss.
For most Australian workers, they're the law.
The Fair Work system.
Most Australian employees are covered by the national system under the Fair Work Act 2009.
It covers nearly all private-sector workers, though some state public servants and local government workers, and many employees of sole traders and partnerships in WA, fall under state systems.
Two bodies do the heavy lifting.
The Fair Work Commission is the independent tribunal that sets minimum wages and awards and hears disputes such as unfair dismissal claims.
The Fair Work Ombudsman gives free advice, helps resolve pay disputes and can take employers to court.
Minimum standards and pay.
The National Employment Standards, NES, are a safety net that no award, agreement or contract can undercut.

They include a maximum of 38 ordinary hours a week for full-time staff, four weeks of paid annual leave, pro rata for part-timers, paid personal and carer's leave, compassionate leave, paid family and domestic violence leave, unpaid parental leave, long service leave, public holidays, and notice and redundancy pay.
Some employees can also request flexible working.
The Fair Work Commission reviews the national minimum wage yearly, usually from 1 July.
Most workers are also covered by a modern award setting pay and conditions, including penalty rates, overtime and breaks.
Enterprise agreements must leave employees better off overall.
Employers must pay superannuation and give you a payslip within one working day of payday.
Casual or permanent.
Employees can be full-time, part-time, casual or fixed-term.
Permanent employees get paid leave and more job security.
Casual employees have no firm advance commitment to ongoing work and usually receive a casual loading instead of paid annual and personal leave, commonly 25 per cent under awards.
Casuals still get some protections, including unpaid carer's leave and, after enough regular service, the right to claim unfair dismissal.
Since 2024, casuals who believe their work has become regular and ongoing can, after a qualifying period, notify their employer that they want to become permanent.
Being wrongly labelled a contractor, called sham contracting, is illegal.
Dismissal and discrimination.
If you are dismissed in a way that is harsh, unjust or unreasonable, you may be able to claim unfair dismissal.
You usually need at least six months' service, or 12 months at an employer with fewer than 15 employees, and some high earners are excluded.
A genuine redundancy isn't unfair dismissal.
The deadline is strict: generally 21 days.
Separately, general protections laws prohibit dismissal because you exercised a workplace right, such as making a complaint or taking leave.
Federal laws make it unlawful to treat workers unfairly because of protected attributes such as race, sex, disability or age, and states have similar laws.
Sexual harassment is unlawful, and since late 2022 employers must take reasonable steps to prevent it.
Complaints can go to the Australian Human Rights Commission or a state body.
Safety and standing up.
Work health and safety laws are made by each state and territory.
Most use harmonised model laws; Victoria has its own similar law.
The business must ensure, so far as is reasonably practicable, the health and safety of workers, including psychological hazards like bullying and excessive workloads.
Workers must take reasonable care too.
You can often cease work that poses a serious risk, and workers' compensation usually covers medical costs and lost wages.
Protect your rights by keeping payslips, rosters, your contract and notes of hours, because underpayment is common and often accidental.
Check your pay with the Fair Work Ombudsman's tools and raise concerns in writing.
Since 2025, intentional underpayment has been a federal crime.
This is general information only; community legal centres, Legal Aid and employment lawyers can advise.
The key idea: The Fair Work Act covers most employees, with the Commission setting minimums and the Ombudsman enforcing them.
Part three. Working on an ABN: contractor or employee.
More Australians are picking up work as contractors.
Here is how to tell if it is genuine, and what to sort out if you go it alone.
Two ways of working.
Liam is offered a job building websites.
The pay is good, but the business asks him to get an ABN and send invoices instead of going on the payroll.
It sounds simple.

Yet the difference between employee and independent contractor changes almost everything: who pays your tax and super, whether you get paid leave, whether an award covers you and what happens if the work dries up.
Plenty of people contract happily, from tradies and consultants to designers, and enjoy the flexibility.
But the label is not just paperwork.
This lesson is general information, not legal, tax or financial advice, so check your own situation with official sources.
Employee or contractor.
There is no single test.
Courts and tribunals look at the whole relationship, including how it works in practice.
Following 2024 changes to the Fair Work Act, the law makes clear that the real substance of the arrangement counts.

Signs of employment include the business controlling how, when and where you work, being paid for your time rather than a result, using their equipment, working only for them, being part of their team and being unable to send someone else.
Signs of genuine contracting include running your own business, choosing how to do the job, taking on financial risk, using your own tools, working for several clients and being able to delegate.
Sham contracting.
Sham contracting is when a business falsely presents employment as independent contracting.
It can be deliberate, to avoid paying super, leave and award rates, or a genuine misunderstanding.

It is against the law to misrepresent employment as contracting, to dismiss an employee in order to re engage them as a contractor doing much the same work, or to pressure someone into becoming a contractor with a false statement.
If you are really an employee, you may be entitled to back pay, super and leave even if you signed a contractor agreement and hold an ABN.
If you are unsure, the Fair Work Ombudsman explains the difference, and the ATO offers an employee or contractor decision tool on its website.
ABN, tax and GST.
If you genuinely carry on a business, you can apply for an Australian Business Number free at abr.
gov.
au, though many websites charge to do it for you.
Employees and hobbyists do not qualify.
Quote it on invoices, as businesses may have to withhold tax from suppliers who do not.
As a contractor, the full invoice usually lands in your account with no tax taken out.
That money is not all yours.
Include it in your tax return, and the ATO may place you on pay as you go instalments.
Many contractors move a set share of each payment into a separate tax account.
You must register for GST once turnover reaches the threshold, or immediately in some industries, such as ride sourcing.
Check current thresholds on the ATO website.
Safety net and pricing.
Genuine contractors often get no paid leave, employer super or workers compensation automatically.
Many make voluntary super contributions, though some contractors paid mainly for their labour can still be entitled to super guarantee payments, so check ATO guidance.
Consider public liability, professional indemnity and income protection insurance, and plan time off.
A common mistake is setting a rate by dividing an employee salary by working hours.
You must also cover super, unpaid leave, insurance, equipment, accounting fees and quiet periods, which is why contract rates often exceed the equivalent wage.
Agree in writing on scope, price, payment terms, who owns the work and how either side can end the deal, and send clear invoices with your ABN.
If a deal feels lopsided, get independent legal advice before signing.
The key idea: Contracting can offer freedom, but it shifts tax, super, leave and risk from the business to you.
Part four. Making a will, and why it matters.
Nobody likes thinking about it, but a will is one of the kindest things you can leave the people you love.
Here is what it does and how to get one right.
Why you need one.
Imagine a couple who have lived together for years but never married, with a child from an earlier relationship.
One dies suddenly without a will.
The partner may face a slow, stressful process to prove the relationship, while assets are divided by a formula in state or territory law, not by what the person wanted.
This is dying intestate.
The rules favour spouses, partners, children and close relatives in a set order, and do not cover friends, charities or stepchildren as many expect.
A will sets out what happens to your estate.
It names beneficiaries and what each receives, including specific gifts, such as a ring to a niece, and the 'residue', which is everything else.
It names an executor to gather assets, pay debts and distribute what is left, and a guardian for children under 18.
Choosing an executor.
Being an executor is not an honour to frame on the wall.
It can mean months of paperwork: locating documents, dealing with banks, possibly applying to the Supreme Court for probate, selling property and settling tax.
Choose someone you trust, who is organised and likely to outlive you, and ask them before naming them.
Many people pick a partner or adult child, often with a backup in case the first cannot act.
Some appoint a professional, such as a solicitor or the state trustee organisation, which charges fees but brings experience and neutrality.
Naming two people who do not get along as joint executors can cause exactly the conflict you hoped to avoid.
Making it valid.
The formal rules vary a little between states and territories, but the core is similar.
The will must be in writing, signed by you, and signed by two adult witnesses who are both present when you sign.
A witness who is also a beneficiary, or a beneficiary's partner, can create problems and the gift to them may be at risk in some places, so use independent witnesses.
Courts can sometimes accept informal documents, but proving them is slow and expensive.
Do-it-yourself kits can work for very simple situations, yet small mistakes are common.
A solicitor is money well spent with blended families, a business, overseas assets or a family member who may contest.
Each state and territory also has a public trustee that can prepare wills, sometimes at low cost.
This is general information, not legal advice.
What a will misses.
Many Australians are surprised that their superannuation does not automatically follow their will.
Super is held in trust, and the fund trustee decides who receives it unless you have made a valid binding death benefit nomination.
Some binding nominations lapse after a few years unless renewed, so check with your fund.
Life insurance held inside super follows the same path.
Property owned as joint tenants, such as a home held jointly by a couple, usually passes straight to the surviving owner regardless of the will.
Bank accounts held jointly can work the same way.
Review these alongside your will, or your careful plan may cover only a fraction of what you own.
Updates and other documents.
Store the original somewhere safe and tell your executor where.
Review it whenever life changes.
In most states, marrying revokes an existing will unless it was made in contemplation of that marriage, and divorce can cancel gifts to a former spouse.
Children, separation, buying property or a beneficiary dying are also reasons to check it.
A will only speaks after death.
If illness left you unable to decide, other documents are needed.
An enduring power of attorney lets someone you trust manage your financial and legal affairs.
An enduring guardianship or similar appointment, with an advance care directive, covers health decisions and records your wishes about treatment.
Forms differ between states, so ask a solicitor.
Talking with your family is uncomfortable for minutes and a gift for years.
The key idea: Without a valid will, law decides who gets what by formula; a will names your beneficiaries, executor and guardian for children.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. What do consumer guarantees mean for a product that fails soon after its warranty ends?
Answer. Goods must be of acceptable quality and last a reasonable time.
Question two. What does the Fair Work Commission do?
Answer. Sets minimum wages and awards, hears disputes.
Question three. What changes when you work as a contractor rather than an employee?
Answer. You handle your own tax and super; leave is not automatic.
Question four. What happens if you die without a valid will?
Answer. State or territory law splits your assets by formula.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
